NINETEEN SIXTY
100,000 LIGHT-YEARS
Take a look at the light switch
on your wall or the smartphone
resting in your hand.
Flipping a switch feels effortless,
yet it draws power from an invisible
web stretching across entire continents.
We split atoms, dam giant rivers,
and beam data through the vacuum of space.
How often do you think about where
all that electricity truly comes from?
From our vantage point on the
ground, human technology looks
almost miraculous.
But how powerful are we when
measured against the terrifying
scale of the cosmos?
If an alien civilization looked
at Earth tonight, what kind of
creature would they see?
In the nineteen sixties,
Soviet astrophysicist Nikolai
Kardashev asked this very question.
Politics, culture, and architecture
would be impossible to read across deep space.
How do you even measure progress
across billions of light-years?
Kardashev proposed a beautifully
simple metric: pure energy consumption.
The more energy a civilization
can capture and control,
the more it can build,
send, and change.
Kardashev divided all potential
civilizations into three massive cosmic tiers.
In the popular version of his scale,
a Type One civilization commands
the entire energy output of its home planet.
A Type Two civilization harnesses
the total power radiated by its parent star.
A Type Three civilization commands
the staggering energy of an entire galaxy.
It sounds like fantasy,
but the idea is simple:
each step needs vastly more power
than the last.
Energy is the currency behind
everything a civilization does,
whether you are boiling water or
traversing the stars.
What would life inside a Type One
civilization actually look like?
It means capturing the sunlight
falling on the world,
along with wind, tidal,
and geothermal power.
Can you imagine waking up in a
world where extreme weather is
simply scheduled?
A Type One society wouldn't just
survive on its planet;
it might manage it like a living organism.
In theory, earthquakes could be
eased before they strike,
hurricanes could be dissipated,
and global climates could be kept in balance.
So, where exactly do we stand on
this monumental ladder?
You might assume our glowing cities
and orbital satellites place us
comfortably near Type One,
but the real number is humbling.
Astronomer Carl Sagan estimated
that humanity sits somewhere around
Type zero point seven.
Our power grids are still vulnerable.
In March of nineteen eighty-nine,
a solar storm blacked out the
electric grid across Quebec.
We still burn the remains of ancient
life for fuel, and extreme weather
can still bring our supply chains
to their knees.
If reaching Type One is difficult,
stepping up to Type Two borders
on the divine.
A Type Two civilization commands
billions of times more power than a Type One.
What kind of engineering would
it take to swallow the light of a star?
In nineteen sixty, physicist Freeman
Dyson suggested that an advanced
civilization could build a vast
swarm of solar collectors
surrounding a sun.
Such a megastructure, popularly
known as a Dyson sphere,
could capture most of a star's output.
Beyond a single solar system lies
the incomprehensible expanse of
the galactic spiral.
A Type Three civilization would
not stop at one sun;
it would harness hundreds of
billions of stars across a hundred
thousand light-years.
Some theoretical models suggest
it might even extract rotational
energy from supermassive black holes.
Traveling between star systems
might be as routine to such a
society as taking a morning train is to you.
To a civilization operating at
this galactic scale, our entire
recorded history might look like
a momentary spark.
Yet this cosmic ladder leaves us
with a chilling paradox.
If energy growth were the natural
path of intelligent life,
why is the cosmos so silent?
Some scientists suspect that the
transition between Type zero and
Type One is a lethal filter that
few species survive, an idea known
as the Great Filter.
Are we clever enough to become
masters of our planet before our
own power consumes us?
We are wielding planetary-scale
technology while still learning
how to cooperate.
We may be living through one of
humanity's greatest tests right now.
Tonight, when you turn off the
light and look up at the night
sky, remember what you are looking at.
That quiet darkness is not empty
space; it is an open frontier
waiting for civilizations that endure.
We are still taking our very first
steps into the cosmos,
but we are looking upward with purpose.
If you want to keep exploring the
grand machinery of our universe,
step inside this lab and subscribe
to Miya's Lab.
Every long journey through the
stars begins with a single curious mind.
